The `mixr` package fits linear mixed-effects
models, centered around the `nlme` package.
It is centered around fitting many models of identical form,
from a list of features as the response variable.


--------------



## Useful functions in `mixr`

* `fit_lme_safely()`
* `fitMixedEffectsModels()`
* `createMixedEffectsTable()`
* `simpleLMEs()`
* `lmeDiagnostic()`
* `simulateLongData()`


-------------------


# Mixed-effects Models
## Model Specification in `R`
The syntax is the same whether using the `nlme` or `lme4` package. R uses 
the Wilkinson notation in specifying model formulas.

#### Random Intercept
```{r, eval = FALSE}
lme(y ∼ time * group, random = ∼1 | pid, data = adat)
```

#### Random Slope
```{r, eval = FALSE}
lme(y ∼ time * group, random = ∼time | pid, data = adat)
```

#### Random Intercept & Random Slope
```{r, eval = FALSE}
lme(y ∼ time * group, random = ∼1 + time | pid, data = adat)
```

#### Syntax Definitions

| Symbol       |                 | Corresponds to |
| ------------ | --------------- |:--------------:|
| $y$          | $\rightarrow$   | $y_{ij}$       |
| $∼ 1$        | $\rightarrow$   | random effects ($b_{0i}$) |
| `pid`        | $\rightarrow$   | field containing the dependent groups (subjects) |
| `time * group` | $\rightarrow$ | fixed effects (with interaction term) |
| `time * group` | $\rightarrow$ | `time + group + time * group` |



--------------


# Example 1: Response to Drug
First, simulate longitudinal data for 20 subjects, having $3-10$ serial
samples each, intercept ($\beta_0 = 1000$), slope ($\beta_1 = 400$),
and a serial autocorrelation parameter of 0.1. The default 
simulation values can be seen below:

```{r args}
args(simulateLongData)
```


```{r simulate_data1, warning = FALSE}
# simulate longitudinal data
# createLongData() is a wrapper for simulateLongData()
p <- list(nsubj = 20, beta0 = 1000, beta1 = 400, max.obs = 10, r.seed = 101,
          sd.pars = list(sigma = 250), auto.cor = 0.1)
ResponseData <- createLongData(subject = p)
ResponseData
table(ResponseData$pid)
```

```{r plot_long_pid, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8}
# plot longitudinal traces by subject ("pid")
ResponseData |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = yij, group = pid, colour = pid)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point( size=4, shape=21, fill="white") +
  ylab(y_lab) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(pid)) +
  ggtitle(bquote(y[ij]~"~"~time))
```

```{r plot_long_combined, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
# plot longitudinal traces together
ResponseData |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = yij, group = pid, colour = pid)) +
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "white") + 
  ylab(y_lab) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Group)) +
  ggtitle(bquote(y[ij]~"~"~time))
```


## Analysis in `R`
The model we wish to fit:
$$
\begin{equation}
   y_{ij} = b_{0i} + \beta_1 time_{ij} + \epsilon_{ij},
\end{equation}
$$

again for the $j^{th}$ observation of the $i^{th}$ subject, where $b_{0i}$ 
is the subject-specific random *intercept*, and $\beta_1$ is the 
fixed-effect for *time*.

```{r fit1}
fit1 <- fit_lme_safely(yij ~ time, random = ~ 1 | pid, data = ResponseData)
summary(fit1)
```

From the fixed-effects column in `Value`, the estimates are reasonably
close to the original parameters:

* $\hat{\beta_0}=$ `r round(summary(fit1)[["tTable"]]["(Intercept)", "Value"], 2)` 
* $\hat{\beta_1}=$ `r round(summary(fit1)[["tTable"]]["time", "Value"], 2)`

Both the slope and intercepts differ significantly from zero.


## `lmeDiagnostic()`
This function allows you to interrogate the subject-specific slope and
intercepts for a given mixed-effects model.

```{r diagnostic, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
lmeDiagnostic(fit1)
```




---------------



# Example 2: Group Dependent Response (Interaction)
In clinical studies, it is often of interest to understand how the treatment
of one group of subjects differs from another group of subjects (e.g. a
control group). In a mixed-model setting, this is accomplished by adding an
interaction term to the model, which sets up a conditional response
variable, given that a subject belongs to a particular group/class.

Next, simulate longitudinal data for 20 subjects, having $3-10$ serial
samples each, intercepts of $\beta_0=1000$, slopes of $\beta_1=0$ (`crtl`)
and $\beta_1=500$ (treat), and a serial autocorrelation parameter of 0.1.
The parameters that differ from the default simulation values can be seen below:

```{r simulate_data2, warning = FALSE}
# simulate longitudinal data with group-specific response
control <- list(nsubj = 20, beta1 = 0, max.obs = 10, r.seed = 10,
                sd.pars = list(sigma = 150), auto.cor = 0.1)
treatment <- list(nsubj = 20, beta1 = 500, max.obs = 10, r.seed = 11,
                  sd.pars = list(sigma = 350), auto.cor = 0.1)
GroupResponseData <- createLongData(control, treatment)
```

Now plot the longitudinal time traces:

```{r plot_long_combined2, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
GroupResponseData |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = yij, group = pid, colour = pid)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
  ylab(y_lab) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Group)) +
  ggtitle(bquote(y[ij]~"~"~time))
```


## Analysis in `R`
The model specification to fit:
$$
\begin{equation}
   y_{ij} = b_{0i} + \beta_1 time_{ij} + \beta_2 group_i + \beta_3 (group_i \times time_{ij}) + \epsilon_{ij},
\end{equation}
$$

again for the $j^{th}$ observation of the $i^{th}$ subject, $b_{0i}$ is
still the subject-specific random intercept and $\beta_1$ is still the
fixed-effect for *time*. However, now there is a fixed-effect for
*group* and an interaction term ($\beta_3$ term) that is multiplied 
by a dummy variable such that:

$$
\begin{equation*}
   G = \begin{cases}
      0, & control \\ 
      1, & treatment
      \end{cases}
\end{equation*}
$$

giving,

$$
\begin{equation}
   y_{ij} = b_{0i} + \beta_1 time_{ij} + \beta_2 group_i + \beta_3 (group_i \times time_{ij}) * G + \epsilon_{ij},
\end{equation}
$$

```{r fit2}
fit2 <- fit_lme_safely(yij ~ time * Group, random = ~ 1 | pid, data = GroupResponseData)
summary(fit2)
```

```{r coef2, echo = FALSE}
# Invisible
tmp <- summary(fit2)$tTable
b0  <- round(tmp["(Intercept)", "Value"], 2)
b1  <- round(tmp["time", "Value"], 2)
b2  <- round(tmp["Grouptreatment", "Value"], 2)
b3  <- round(tmp["time:Grouptreatment", "Value"], 2)
t1  <- round(tmp["time:Grouptreatment", "t-value"], 2)
```

From the fixed-effects column in `Value`, the estimates are reasonably close
to the original parameters:

* $\hat{\beta_0}=$ `r b0`
* $\hat{\beta_1}=$ `r b1` (essentially zero).

This indicates that the effect of time has no effect on $y_{ij}$ 
(at least for the controls!).
The significant **interaction** tells a different story and indicates
that the **entire** fixed-effect for *time* occurs in the *treatment*
group ($\hat{\beta_3}=$ `r b3`); in this case the *control* group does
not vary with time.


--------------


# Specific Functions
## Mixed-effects Tables
Fitting mixed-effects models on an `soma_adat` object is achieved via
the `fitMixedEffectsModels()` function. In this toy example, we will use
the `lme_data` object that has longitudinal time series data. Typically
for such analyses, you must identify 4 fields of information:

* Time  (x-axis)
* Response (usually the feature; y-axis)
* Subject identifier
* Group (optional; if a group-wise interaction is desired)

In the example below, we will fit a model with random offsets, i.e. allowing
the intercept to vary by subject with respect to time:

```{r fit_mixed}
options(width = 110)
models <- lme_data |>
  fitMixedEffectsModels(fixed = "TimePoint*Response", random = "~ 1 | Pop")
purrr::map(models, summary)
```

The next step is to convert these models into a univariate table similar to
the `calc.*` family from `SomaClassify`. This is obviously a toy example with
only 2 features, but the same syntax is easily scaled to 1000s of features

```{r}
createMixedEffectsTable(models)
```



## `simpleLMEs()`
Also fits simple linear mixed-effects models wrapping around `fit_lme_safely()`,
however with some defaults around a _slope_ random effect (`time` is typically
either a fixed only or both fixed and random effect).

An additional feature is that you may optionally compare two data sets for 
significant effects by passing a list of data frames as the `data =` argument.

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
data1 <- simulateLongData(r.seed = 101, beta1 = 50)
model <- simpleLMEs(data1, "yij", "time", "pid")

# S3 print method
model

# S3 plot method
plot(model)

# plot only certain subject traces
plot(model, groups = c(1, 3, 5, 10))

# random offset
model2 <- simpleLMEs(data1, "yij", "time", "pid", random.slope = FALSE)
model2

# 2 data set option
data2 <- simulateLongData(r.seed = 405, beta1 = 10)     # smaller beta1
model3 <- simpleLMEs(list(A = data1, B = data2), "yij", "time", "pid")

# S3 print method
model3
```

## `simulateLongData()`
Simulate 1 response variable with some covariance structure within the 
subjects.

* pid: subject identifier
* time: time point
* yij: response for the $j^{th}$ measurement of the $i^{th}$ subject

```{r simulate}
simulateLongData()
```

There is also a convenient wrapper to generate simulated longitudinal data
in a group-wise fashion.

## `createLongData()`
```{r create_sim1}
control   <- list(nsubj = 20, beta1 = 10, max.obs = 10, r.seed = 10, auto.cor = 0.1)
treatment <- list(nsubj = 20, beta1 = 500, max.obs = 10, r.seed = 11, auto.cor = 0.1)
createLongData(control, treatment)
```

You may also change the group names by passing labels explicitly:

```{r create_sim2}
createLongData(GroupA = control, GroupB = treatment)
```
